newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Sinn Fein challenges UK over election.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein challenges UK over election.

text.p: The IRA's political wing Sinn Fein on Sunday challenged the winner of British elections on May 1 to lift a ban on its entry to Northern Ireland peace talks and negotiate a lasting settlement.

Gerry Adams, the Sinn Fein president, told a one-day party conference that Sinn Fein votes in the elections would put pressure on the British government and pro-British Unionist parties to end the ban and talk.

"The Westminster (British parliament) elections on May 1 are a watershed moment in our history that must be seized. We must send a clear message to the government and the Unionist leadership," Adams told around 500 delegates in the border town of Monaghan.

Sinn Fein is contesting 17 of the 18 Northern Ireland constituencies and is confident of winning two to three seats, which would present the next British government with the dilemma of refusing to talk to elected representatives.

Britain, Ireland and the United States have banned all contact with Sinn Fein since the Iish Republican Army ended a 17-month ceasefire in its war against British rule in Northern Ireland in February 1996.

The three governments said there could be no contact with and no Sinn Fein participation in the Belfast peace talks until the IRA restores its ceasefire and declares a permanent end to its 28-year war.
But Sinn Fein delegates said they thought that if Britain's opposition Labour Party ousts Prime Minister John Major's Conservatives, it might ease the ban.

"Every vote for Sinn Fein increases the pressure on the incoming British government to engage in a process of real and credible negotiations involving all of the parties," Sinn Fein's chief negotiator, Martin McGuinness, told delegates.
"A strong mandate for Sinn Fein will reverberate throughout the corridors of power in Dublin, London and Washington as well as in European capitals," he said.
"It will bring untold pressure to bear on the incoming British government and the Irish government to engage in a credible process of inclusive peace negotiations,"he added.

McGuinness and Adams made no mention of the party's policy of refusing to occupy seats it wins in the British parliament because it would entail allegiance to Britain, which sees it sees as the illegal colonial ruler of Northern Ireland.

Nor was there any hint of a new IRA ceasefire. McGuinness said only that Sinn Fein wanted the Belfast talks, which group pro-British Unionists and pro-Irish nationalists, "to take place in a peaceful atmosphere".

Media reports suggest the IRA may call a truce after the election in a bid to get Sinn Fein to the peace talks which are due to resume on June 3 under the chairmanship of former U.S. Senator George Mitchell.
Sinn Fein won 15 percent of votes in an election to a non-executive peace forum last May, its best showing in a Northern Ireland election, and hopes both McGuinness and Adams will win seats on May 1.

Sinn Fein's ideological foes, Unionists who want Northern Ireland to stay British, say they will never negotiate a settlement to a war which has killed 3,200 until the IRA gives up violence for good and embraces democratic politics.

The conference, in the Irish border town of Monaghan, took place 24 hours after the IRA claimed responsibility for two small bombs on British railway networks and a series of bomb hoaxes which created transport havoc last week.
Major and his likely successor, Labour Party leader Tony Blair, both condemned the attacks and said the IRA would get nowhere until it ended violence for good.
